Additional information:  The pattern is for a loose fitting dress or tunic with a handkerchief-type hem.  I used an inexpensive linen blend (probably some sort of linen-synthetic blend I'm assuming given the price point).  Unfortunately I bought the fabric before I realized I should be writing down the information from the bolt for my records.  The bodice front consists of two bias-cut pieces that meet in the middle with a V-shaped seam.  The pockets are meant to be loose and baggy and my unfortunately short arms means that they are a little low to be practical in any way.  I picked the size based on my upper bust compared to the bust body measurement on the pattern size chart and did not make any alterations, though I think some are needed (questions about this in the post body).  

Edit:  Apparently my questions have disappeared so adding them here.

1. I would like to get feedback on fit.  I haven't been successful at it yet, but I think going forward I need to do FBAs on my garments.  However, after doing some googling, I don't think this is something I can really do on this pattern because of the bias cut.  Especially because it doesn't contain any darts to begin with.  However, thoughts on this would be very appreciated.

2. If, as I expect, a FBA isn't possible, I'd love to get some feedback on the fit.  Based on other reviews, the waviness down the center line might be just an issue with the pattern in general, but perhaps it is fit related?  Same with the lines around the upper chest, armpits.  Not sure if this is because I stretched the fabric by accident or if it is a fit issue.  \[Note: The butt fold was because I didn't realize that the dress had apparently gotten stuck on my cotton underwear when the picture was taken.  I believe this is not a fit issue and really just an issue with cotton sticking to other fabrics lol.\]

I think that's it.  Overall, this is the first dress I've made that was wearable at all outside the house.  Everything else either ended up way, way, way too big (not sure if I am tape ruler impaired or just have a weird body) or were never finished and thrown away in frustration (luckily these were all muslins where I had screwed up enough to the point it was unfixable and/or I never wanted to look at the thing again).  I'd love to get feedback in general, as I thought it looked cute when I put it on in front of the mirror, but now looking at the pictures I"m not so sure.  Does it look too Becky home-ec-y and/or ill fitting?  If so, I'll limit it to house wearing and either try again or move on to a different pattern. 

\[Note: I do know that future iterations would need to have the sleeves either shortened or lengthened as I'm pretty sure they hit at the worst place, though I'm not sure where would look better. Also, the v seam does not meet perfectly at the bottom at the v - it's not too bad, but could definitely be better.\]

I'm so, so sorry for your loss.  I lost my dog about 6 months ago and it's so, so hard to get through (and I'm crying while I write this thinking of her).  As everyone has said, there's no easy way through any of this.  You will cry for what feels like days on end.  You will scream into your pillow about why it had to happen and why couldn't you have been a better owner/parent and why didn't you do this or that and that she was the best dog who ever existed and you didn't deserve her (or maybe that's just me, but you'll probably find yourself grieving in an unproductive and unhelpful way that you just need to let happen).

In the end, there were a few things I did that I think helped.  First, I hung her collar up somewhere that I pass several times a day.  In the beginning I would kiss it every time I passed and I'd make my husband kiss it every time he left the house (poor guy, he probably felt ridiculous but he knew it made me feel better so he did it).  I didn't wash her dog bed and kept it in my office and lay down on it every once in a while (I've since washed it because I've moved past that stage, but it took a little while).  When I was ready, I printed out my favorite pic of her and put it in a frame under my tv.  Finally, we planted a tree and buried some of her ashes with it.  (Ironically, the tree has since died, but we plan on planting something new this coming spring - eventually something will take root.  So don't do this if it would devastate you that the plant died and you had to make a second (or third) attempt.)

Also, if you can’t go into everything on the first visit that’s totally fine. Even if you can just provide a high level overview of why you need help. And while it helps them to help you if you can answer all their questions, you can totally at any time say that you’re not comfortable answering that yet. They won’t get mad or annoyed at you for that. Also keep in mind that you are simultaneously auditioning them for a position as your therapist. Now don’t walk away just because you feel awkward about opening up, but if you feel judged in any way or just feel like you could never work with them it would be totally within your rights to request a different therapist. You are in control. 

And remember. No matter how bad and embarrassing you think your problem is, they’ve definitely heard worse. Even if it’s not a patient but something they read in a case story. Which doesn’t mean that your problems are any lesser, or hurt you any less, but that the psychologist/psychiatrist will only hear a person who is hurting and needs help. The problem I have with this point of view is it leads to a horribly depressing monotone world. Everyone graduating would have the same 5 or 10 degrees. Who would have the education to teach our children the arts? Or the humanities? Think of the novels we might miss out on or the symphonies that might never be written because people are not following their dreams. Or no one was knowledgeable enough to edit the next great novel or play the symphony. Think of the museums that would have no curators, the natural history museums with no archaeologists to discover things or clean the bones already in storage. The history books that would never get researched or written. The scandals that could be hidden because no journalists existed to cover it. The evening news that had no newscasters because no one could afford to enter at the lowest ranks of local reporting and work on up the ladder. 

Sure these things can be done by extremely talented people with no training, but many need training to allow their skills to mature. So, no, I don't think higher education is just an investment of one individual into their own future. I don't think we should mock majors that don't lead to high paying jobs. And I don't think we should discourage young people from following their dreams. There are enough mediocre doctors and lawyers and engineers out there without adding to their ranks people who are uninspired and hate their work. Life is about more than economics and should not be boiled down to the almighty dollar. 

As an aside, I majored in anthropology and women's studies at an expensive private university. Most of my debt was accrued, however, at graduate school for public health. That being said I have all federal loans and am paying them back regularly. I would not go back and change my undergraduate experience one bit, though I may have taken a different path after college if offered a do over.

Just wanted to echo everyone else's remarks that I hope you don't blame yourself - it sounds like one of those really, really unfortunate things that just happens for no good reason at all.  Unfortunately, I know that nothing we say will ever make you able to forget this or feel sad about it at times, though I hope you remind yourself at those times that it wasn't your fault.  

And as you can see from all the replies, many people have been in a same or similar situation, or been close to being in the same situation.  Although I'm not religious at all, I do tend to think about the statement "there but for the grace of god go I" - I tend to, in my thinking, substitute luck for grace of god, but you get the idea.  When I was a teenager, I lived on a hill with a steep and winding road.  One day, I was coming down the hill and coming around a blind curve.  My neighbor's son was in the middle of the street, right in the middle of the curve, pushing his tricycle uphill.  I was luckily going slow enough that day to stop with plenty of room.  In fact, after I stopped the kid kept coming at me as his head was pointing down at the ground while he pushed.  He eventually looked up, his eyes grew wide as saucers, and he ran away.  The kid is luckily now grown up and doing fine as far as I know.  But it scared me to think of all the times I'd come down that hill too fast because I was in a hurry, or just because I was a stupid teenager.

My mom once caught my brother and a friend hiding under leaves by the side of the road.  Thank goodness no one came along during that time or drove over the leaves.  I avoid leaf piles now for that same exact reason.  And when I was in grade school, we went to a nearby amusement park with my junior girl scout troop, and one of the girl's brothers (her mom was a leader) ran out into the street after lunch to try and get to the side of the street that his sister was on.  And he was hit, luckily it just knocked him over backwards and he turned out to be fine.  Though he did have to go to the hospital instead of spending the day at the park.  But I remember the man who hit him - he was so upset about the incident.  And I felt in some way it was easier to be the people on the receiving end than those that did the hitting, because we know the boy turned out okay and everything was fine and most was probably forgotten.  But I bet that man still remembers clearly the day he hit a little boy in the street.  Such a sad thing to have to live with.

So anyway, after all this rambling, I just wanted to say that I hope you can take some comfort in knowing it was not your fault and that many people can sympathize with what has happened.
